parts.title: Part 1
parts.context: A man books a stall at a craft fair.
script: Hello, Winter Craft Fair, Bridget speaking.
Hi. I'd like to book a stall at the craft fair.
Lovely. Can I take your name?
Ali Hassan. H, A, double S, A, N.
That's perfect for a winter fair. As you probably know, the fair is on Saturday the twenty-third of November.
Yes. What size are the stalls?
Each stallholder gets a two-metre table.
Is it possible to choose where my stall is?
Most of the spaces near the entrance have gone, but there's space near the stage, where there'll be live music all day.
Near the stage would be great. Lots of people will stop there.
The stall fee is thirty-five pounds.
Yes. All stallholders must have public liability insurance. You'll need to send us a copy before the fair.
OK. What time can I set up?
The hall opens at eight a.m. for stallholders, and the public arrive at ten.
Is there electricity at the stalls? I wanted to light the display.
I'm afraid not. Most people use lights that run on batteries.
Right. And will you be advertising the fair?
Yes, and we'll feature all our stallholders in our newsletter, which goes to about three thousand people.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.context: A student union officer welcomes new students.
script: Hi everyone, and welcome to the university. I'm Daniel, the president of the Student Union this year.
The Student Union is run by students, for students. All the officers are elected by students every spring, and anyone can stand for election.
Every student automatically becomes a member, and membership is free. You don't need to sign anything.
Our most popular service by far is the Job Shop, which helps students find part-time work, both on and off campus.
During exam periods, the main union building stays open until midnight, so you can study there in the evenings.
Let me tell you where to find things. The Job Shop is on the first floor of the union building.
The Advice Centre, which can help with problems such as housing, money or difficulties with your course, is on the ground floor, right by the main entrance.
Our second-hand bookshop is in the basement. It's a great place to buy textbooks cheaply.
The quiet room, for prayer or reflection, is also on the first floor, at the end of the corridor.
The bike repair workshop is in a small building next to the library.
And the clubs and societies office is in the sports centre, since many of the clubs are sports clubs.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.context: Two students, Tara and Rahim, discuss a survey of reading habits.
script: Tara, let's look at the results of our reading habits survey for the city library.
Yes. It's good to be working on a real project. The library asked for the survey because they're planning their budget for next year.
We got five hundred responses, which is a good sample.
What surprised me most was the teenagers. I assumed they'd mostly read on screens, but they read far more printed books than I expected.
Me too. The main problem with the survey was that very few retired people answered, because it was online.
We should mention that as a limitation. What should we recommend?
I think the library should start an audiobook service. A lot of people said they'd like one.
Agreed. Let's go through the preferred formats for each group. Under-eighteens, as I said, prefer printed books.
University students prefer e-books, mainly because they're cheaper and easy to carry.
Commuters prefer audiobooks. They listen while driving or on the bus.
The few retired people who answered prefer print.
And parents of young children prefer audiobooks too, because they can listen while doing other things.

parts.title: Part 4
script: Today we're looking at one of the most remarkable societies in the animal world: leafcutter ants, which are found in Central and South America.

As their name suggests, these ants cut pieces of leaf and carry them back to their nests. But they don't eat the leaves. Instead, they use them to grow a fungus, which is their main source of food. In other words, they are farmers.
Leafcutter colonies can be enormous. A single colony may contain up to eight million ants, and the underground nest can be many metres deep.
Each colony is founded by a single queen, who can live for around fifteen years, laying millions of eggs.

The workers are divided into different castes, mainly according to their size. Large workers act as soldiers, medium-sized ones cut and carry leaves, and the smallest ones look after the fungus garden.
Some of the tiny workers ride on the pieces of leaf as they are carried home. Their job is to protect the carriers from parasitic flies, which try to lay eggs on the larger ants.
The ants also have to protect their fungus from disease. Bacteria living on their bodies produce antibiotics, which kill harmful moulds.
Waste from the fungus garden is carried to special chambers, away from the rest of the nest, to prevent the spread of disease.
Because they can strip crops of their leaves very quickly, leafcutter ants are considered major agricultural pests in some areas.
Remarkably, studies suggest that ants have been farming fungus for around fifty million years, far longer than humans have been farming crops.

passages.title: Building the Great Pyramid
paragraphs: The Great Pyramid of Giza was built around 2560 BC for the pharaoh Khufu. Originally about 146 metres high, it remained the tallest human-made structure in the world for nearly 4,000 years. It contains an estimated 2.3 million blocks of stone, some weighing several tonnes, and its sides are aligned almost exactly with the points of the compass.

For a long time, it was popularly believed that the pyramids were built by slaves. Archaeological discoveries have changed this picture. In 1990, archaeologists discovered the tombs of pyramid workers close to the Giza plateau. These people were buried with honour near the king's monument, which slaves would not have been. Evidence from a nearby settlement shows that the workers were well fed, receiving bread, beer and meat, and some skeletons show signs of medical care for injuries. Most historians now believe that the pyramids were built by paid labourers and by teams of farmers who worked for limited periods.

In 2013, archaeologists working at Wadi al-Jarf, an ancient harbour on the Red Sea, discovered the oldest inscribed papyri ever found in Egypt. Among them was a logbook kept by an official named Merer, who led a team of around 40 men. It describes how they transported blocks of fine limestone by boat along the Nile and canals from quarries at Tura to Giza, where the stone was used for the pyramid's smooth outer casing. Most of the pyramid's core, however, was built from limestone quarried on the Giza plateau itself.

How the blocks were raised remains debated. Most theories involve ramps, either straight, zigzagging or spiralling around the pyramid. In 2018, archaeologists at an ancient alabaster quarry called Hatnub discovered a steep ramp with staircases and post holes on either side, suggesting that blocks were pulled up using a system of ropes and posts. The ramp dates from Khufu's reign, but it is not known whether the same technique was used at Giza.

Moving the blocks across the desert was also a challenge. A 2014 study by physicists in Amsterdam showed that wetting the sand in front of a sledge reduces the force needed to pull it by about half, because damp sand does not pile up in front of the sledge. An ancient Egyptian wall painting appears to show exactly this: a worker pouring water in front of a sledge carrying a giant statue.

Despite these discoveries, many questions remain. The pyramids are a reminder of the remarkable organisation, skill and knowledge of a civilisation that, without iron tools or wheels for heavy transport, produced structures that still stand more than four and a half thousand years later.

passages.title: The Race to the South Pole
paragraphs: In the southern summer of 1911, two expeditions set out across Antarctica with the same goal: to be the first to reach the South Pole. One was led by the Norwegian explorer Roald Amundsen, the other by the British naval officer Robert Falcon Scott. Their contrasting approaches, and their very different fates, have been studied and debated ever since.

Amundsen prepared meticulously. During earlier expeditions in the Arctic, he had spent time with Inuit people and learned from their methods of survival. He adopted their loose fur clothing, which kept travellers warm without causing them to sweat, and he relied on teams of sled dogs, which were fast and could cope with extreme cold. His team also included expert skiers.

Scott chose a different strategy. He took motor sledges, Siberian ponies and some dogs. The motor sledges broke down soon after the journey began, and the ponies, which sank into the snow and could not survive the cold, had to be shot. For much of the journey, Scott and his men had to pull their heavy sledges themselves, a method known as man-hauling, which was exhausting and slow.

Amundsen's team reached the Pole on 14 December 1911. Scott's party of five arrived more than a month later, on 17 January 1912, to find a Norwegian tent and a letter left by Amundsen. Scott wrote in his diary of his bitter disappointment.

The return journey ended in tragedy. Weakened by hunger and cold, and slowed by unusually severe weather, Scott and his companions died one by one. The last three, including Scott, died in their tent only about 18 kilometres from a supply depot. Their bodies, together with Scott's diaries, were found by a search party in November 1912.

In Britain, Scott was celebrated for decades as a national hero who had died bravely. Later historians criticised his planning, arguing that Amundsen's focus on proven methods was far wiser. More recently, some researchers have pointed out that the weather Scott faced was exceptionally harsh, and that his expedition carried out valuable scientific work. Even on the return journey, his men continued to carry rock samples, which later provided important evidence about Antarctica's geological history.

passages.title: Can We Trust the Experts?
paragraphs: In recent years, it has become common for politicians and commentators to express doubt about experts. During a debate in the United Kingdom in 2016, a senior politician famously claimed that people had 'had enough of experts'. Such remarks reflect a wider loss of confidence in the authority of scientists, economists and other specialists. Is this scepticism justified?

There are certainly reasons for caution. In 2015, a large project attempted to repeat 100 published experiments in psychology. Fewer than half produced the same results as the original studies. Similar problems have been found in other fields, including medicine and economics. This 'replication crisis' does not mean that all research is unreliable, but it does show that individual studies should be treated with care.

Experts are also often poor at predicting the future. In a famous study, the psychologist Philip Tetlock collected thousands of forecasts from political and economic experts over many years. He found that, on average, their predictions were only slightly better than chance, and that the most famous experts were often among the least accurate.

Yet in other areas, expertise is extremely valuable. Weather forecasting is a striking example. Modern five-day forecasts are as accurate as one-day forecasts were a few decades ago. The difference is that weather forecasters receive regular, clear feedback: they find out within days whether their predictions were right, and they can use this information to improve their models. Fields in which experts are frequently tested against reality tend to produce more reliable judgements.

The COVID-19 pandemic illustrated both the importance and the difficulty of expert advice. Scientists developed vaccines with remarkable speed, but changing guidance on issues such as masks led some people to conclude that experts did not know what they were doing. In fact, changing advice in response to new evidence is how science is supposed to work. The problem was often that early advice had been presented with more certainty than the evidence justified.

In my view, the answer is neither blind trust nor blanket rejection. Our trust should be calibrated, depending on the field and on the track record of the experts involved. Experts, for their part, should be open about uncertainty, explaining not only what they think but how confident they are. And the public should learn to see changing advice not as a sign of incompetence, but as evidence that experts are responding to new information.

task1.text: The bar chart below shows the number of hot drinks and ice creams sold by a café in six months of one year. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words.
model: The bar chart compares the number of hot drinks and ice creams sold by a café in January, March, May, July, September and November of one year.

Overall, sales of the two products followed opposite seasonal patterns. Hot drinks sold best in the colder months at the beginning and end of the year, whereas ice cream sales peaked in summer. Hot drinks were the more popular product in every month except July.

In January, the café sold 900 hot drinks but only 50 ice creams. Hot drink sales then fell steadily, to 750 in March and 500 in May, reaching a low of 300 in July. At the same time, ice cream sales rose sharply, from 120 in March to 400 in May and a peak of 800 in July, when they were more than double the figure for hot drinks.
In the second half of the year, the trends reversed. Hot drink sales recovered to 550 in September and 850 in November, while ice cream sales dropped to 350 and then to just 80.

task2.text: Some people think that international travel should be limited because of its effect on the environment. To what extent do you agree or disagree? Write at least 250 words.
model: International travel has grown enormously in recent decades, and with it the environmental costs, particularly the carbon emissions from aviation. Some people therefore argue that travel abroad should be limited. While I agree that the environmental impact of travel must be reduced, I do not believe that strict limits on travel are the right solution.

There are strong reasons to be concerned. Aviation is one of the fastest-growing sources of greenhouse gas emissions, and a single long-haul return flight can produce more carbon per passenger than many people in developing countries produce in a year. Mass tourism also damages fragile environments, from coral reefs to mountain trails, and puts pressure on water and energy supplies in popular destinations. Without action, these problems will grow as more people can afford to travel.

However, limiting travel would have serious drawbacks. Millions of people in developing countries depend on tourism for their income, and many families are separated by migration and rely on flights to see each other. Travel also has educational and cultural value, helping people understand other ways of life. Moreover, limits would be most likely to affect people on lower incomes, while the wealthy could continue to travel freely.

A better approach is to make travel more sustainable. Governments can tax aviation fuel and frequent flyers, invest in high-speed rail as an alternative to short flights, and support research into cleaner aircraft. Individuals can also choose to travel less often but stay longer, and to prefer trains where possible.

In conclusion, although the environmental damage caused by travel is serious, I believe it should be addressed through taxes, cleaner technology and better alternatives, rather than by limiting people's freedom to travel.

speaking.cue:
Describe something you bought that you were very happy with.
You should say:
- what it was
- where you bought it
- why you bought it
and explain why you were happy with it.
speaking.cueModel: I'd like to talk about a second-hand laptop I bought at the beginning of my second year at university. My old laptop was very slow, and it had started to crash whenever I ran programming software, which was a real problem for a computer science student. New laptops with the specifications I needed were far too expensive, so a senior student suggested I look at refurbished ones. I found a shop in Elephant Road in Dhaka that sells used laptops which have been checked and repaired, and after comparing a few, I chose a three-year-old business laptop with a good processor and plenty of memory. It cost less than half the price of a new one, and the shop gave me a six-month warranty. I was a bit nervous at first, because you never know with second-hand electronics, but it's been fantastic. It's fast, the keyboard is comfortable for long coding sessions, and the battery lasts most of the day. I'm happy with it partly because it works so well, but also because I made a sensible decision. I saved a lot of money, and buying a refurbished laptop is better for the environment than buying a new one.
